The Seljuk Empire. From 1037 to 1194 of the common era, this was a Turkish dynasty descended from the Oghuz nomads, which conquered Central Asia, Persia, and Anatolia, becoming the dominant military power in the Islamic world. Under sultans like Alp Arslan and Nizam al-Mulk, the Seljuks revitalized the weakened Abbasid caliphate, established Persian cultural norms across their vast realm, and clashed with Crusader armies in the Holy Land.

The Seljuks were founded by Seljuk ibn Duqaq in 1037. They expanded rapidly under Alp Arslan and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who reorganized the state with a sophisticated bureaucracy and military hierarchy. In 1071, at the Battle of Manzikert, they defeated a Byzantine army—a pivotal victory that opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and led the Byzantine emperor to make a desperate appeal to the Pope. This became a trigger for the Crusades. By the twelfth century the Seljuks had fragmented into competing atabegs, or military governors, in Syria and Mesopotamia, losing central cohesion even as individual Turkish emirates remained powerful. They patronized Islamic scholarship and architecture. Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyyah madrasas, institutions of learning that became models for Islamic universities across the medieval world. They reconstituted Sunni orthodoxy by supporting the Abbasid caliph—though holding supreme power themselves—and championed Sunni jurisprudence against Shiite rivals. After Nizam al-Mulk's assassination in 1092, the empire declined further, weakened by Crusader incursions and internal fragmentation. It was eventually succeeded by regional successors like the Zengids.

The Abbasid Caliphate was the theoretical overlord they supported against Shiite rivals. The Crusades were the military conflicts Seljuk expansion inadvertently sparked. The Battle of Manzikert in 1071 transformed Anatolia. And the Ghaznavid Dynasty was a related Turkish power that preceded them in Central Asia.
